newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela vows to uncover truth of Machel air crash.
newsitem.headline: Mandela vows to uncover truth of Machel air crash.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela vowed on Thursday to leave no stone unturned in finding the truth behind the air crash 10 years ago which killed Mozambican leader Samora Machel.

Speaking on a dusty hillside hard-by the South African and Mozambican border, with Machel's widow Graca present, Mandela made clear he believed the Mozambican president was murdered by agents of the South African apartheid regime.
"Certainty about the precise chain of events which robbed Africa of one of its greatest leaders still eludes us," Mandela said in a speech marking the 10th anniversary at the site of the crash.

"We do know however, that at that time, savage wounds were being inflicted on our beloved southern Africa by the apartheid war machine. No corner of the region was spared the cruelty and... barbarity of the defenders of this crime against humanity.
"No country that identified with the yearning of the South African people, no leader who expressed practical solidarity with them, was spared," Mandela said.
"We shall leave no stone unturned to ensure that, in the fullness of time, nothing but the whole truth is known about these events."

Machel and over 30 others were killed on October 19, 1986 en route to Maputo on a government flight, when their Soviet- piloted aircraft crashed inexplicably into low hills right on the Mozambique-South Africa border.

Anti-apartheid forces fighting the white regime at the time said they suspected that Machel, a close supporter of their movement, was deliberately killed when his plane was lured off- course by a false radar beacon planted by South African agents.

An official investigation subsequently declared the crash a result of pilot error. But on his first state visit to the crash site three years ago, Mandela said he did not believe the findings and he was determined to resume the investigation.
Machel's successor, President Joachim Chissano, said his country would support all South african efforts to ensure "that the truth comes to light about the tragedy".
Fighting back tears, Graca Machel placed a wreath at the simple monument on the spot where her husband's body was found.

She and Mandela, who made their love affair public last month, remained at a discreet distance from each other during the ceremony. Mandela declined to pose for photographers with her, saying it would be inappropriate.
